target_only_tests.why: Twenty, all of them about `src/cli/parser.ts`, `src/cli.ts` and the one repair in `src/measurement/cli.ts` -- code this port had to write because Node has no argparse, and which therefore carries no warrant from interlock (rule 11). Five of the thirteen exist because something could not see the property it named. Two came from the mutation sweep: `the help walk reaches the mounted subcommand's own flags` closes the hazard that both cp932 cases are a loop over helpStrings and a walk returning nothing makes both vacuously green, and `half a corpus reference is refused for being half` closes an inherited blind spot -- the ported case (and its source) point --fixture-corpus at a directory that does not exist, so loadCorpus refuses with a FixtureRefusal, which IS a ControlPlaneRefusal, and the case stays green with the half-reference guard deleted (measured). Nine came from the review gate, in four rounds. Round 1: Python's `int()` accepts underscores between digits so the source's parser takes `--period-start-ms 1_700_000_000_000` and the port's first parser refused it; a nested command's refusal named the root parser above a usage line naming the child; and a missing or malformed shadow file escaped as a raw filesystem error or SyntaxError rather than as the refusal the function documents. Round 2 found the two the port had that argparse does not: `--flag=value` is argparse's other spelling of `--flag value` and this parser took only one of them, and the entry-point guard compared `process.argv[1]` unresolved -- which is the symlink npm publishes a `bin` as, so the installed command exited 0 having run nothing and printed nothing while `node dist/cli.js` worked. Round 3 found the one accepted command line that produces a wrong report rather than no report: with a value omitted, `--fixture-commit --format json` took `--format` as the commit the labelled corpus came from and rendered in the default format, so the operator gets a plausible report whose provenance is false -- and nothing downstream can catch it, because a commit is an opaque string and the default format is valid. argparse refuses this and now so does the port, with `--flag=--literal` as the escape hatch and a negative number still a value, which `--grace-ms -1` depends on. Round 4 raised no P1 and two P2s: `--version=x` printed the version and exited 0 while argparse refuses a value handed to a zero-argument action, now matched including argparse's wording; and Python's `int()` accepts any Unicode decimal digit, which this parser refuses -- a divergence taken deliberately rather than closed, and pinned as one (see divergences). One more came from the Windows CI cells rather than from the review gate -- see the D-0109 note in `entries` below -- and reproduces on POSIX the escaping the Windows paths made visible. The remaining eight pin the parser's own refusals: a required flag, a value outside a flag's choices, a flag given twice, three spellings of a non-integer millisecond value, --help routed to the subcommand rather than the root, and the version flag.

approved_non_running.reason: Target-only, and each skipped where the hazard does not exist. (1) `the CLI runs when it is invoked through a bin symlink` drives the built CLI through a symlink, which is how npm publishes a `bin` on Unix: `node_modules/.bin/continuo` is a link, Node sets process.argv[1] to it, and an entry-point guard that does not resolve it is false for every installed user. On Windows npm writes a `.cmd` shim that invokes node with the real path, so argv[1] is already resolved and there is nothing to catch; creating a file symlink there also needs a privilege the CI cells are not guaranteed to hold. (2) `a db path that needs escaping is printed escaped` puts a backslash in a directory name, which is legal on POSIX and illegal on Windows. It exists to make the Windows failure visible on the machines this belt is developed on, so running it on Windows is neither possible nor the point. In both cases the property is not left unguarded on the skipped platform -- there is nothing there to guard.
approved_non_running.approved_by: worker, 2026-08-28, on the codex review gate's P1

entries.reason: D-0113. Node has no cp932 encoder, so `text.encode('cp932')` has no counterpart. entries.target_id: test/measurement/cli.test.ts::cp932 > help runs in a real console and writes only ASCII bytes
entries.reason: D-0113. The source sets PYTHONIOENCODING=cp932 so the child's stdout raises on a character it cannot encode; Node writes UTF-8 whatever the console is, so there is no stream encoding to set and no exception to provoke. The port checks the bytes that actually left the process instead -- `--help` must write only bytes below 0x80, which are the same bytes in cp932 -- and keeps the source's other two assertions (exit 0, `--fingerprint` present) unchanged. It drives the BUILT dist/cli.js, which is why the case asserts that file exists first: section 10 instance 1 is the same subprocess-without-a-build hazard.

divergences.behaviour: The CLI is parsed by a purpose-built parser rather than by argparse, and it accepts less than argparse does: long flags only (in both of argparse's spellings, `--flag value` and `--flag=value`), one value each (and a next-token value that reads as a flag is refused, as argparse refuses it), no positional arguments, no prefix matching, no nargs. It also refuses one command line argparse accepts -- a flag given twice, which argparse resolves by keeping the last value. Python's own integer spelling is matched rather than approximated, underscores between digits included.

The two cp932 help-string cases assert ASCII rather than cp932-encodability, and the subprocess case checks the bytes `--help` wrote rather than setting the child's stdout encoding. Node has neither a cp932 encoder nor a PYTHONIOENCODING equivalent.
`the command opens no writable connection` asserts the driver's readonly open flag rather than a `mode=ro` URI. Recorded here because this case is the one that asserts it on the whole call path.
The top-level CLI mounts one subtree where interlock's mounts six; the other five name modules continuo has not ported.
A missing or malformed v1 shadow input file refuses with a ControlPlaneRefusal naming the path, where the source lets the filesystem's or the JSON parser's own error escape.

A millisecond flag refuses a non-ASCII decimal digit. Python's int() accepts any Unicode Nd digit -- int('１２') is 12, int('१२') is 12 -- so the source's parser takes a full-width timestamp and this one does not.
divergences.note: Taken deliberately rather than closed. The value is an epoch millisecond the report prints in its header, so decoding '１２' produces a document saying '12' that the operator cannot reproduce from what they typed; and decoding correctly needs a Unicode digit-value table (NFKD folds the full-width forms and not the Devanagari ones) whose failure mode is a silently wrong number rather than an error, which is the class rule 11 names. The refusal is fail-visible and quotes what it got -- the right answer on the Japanese console D-0113 is about, where an IME left in full-width mode is the likely cause. Pinned by a target-only case so it stays deliberate.

divergences.behaviour: `header.db_path` and `v1_shadow.source` are printed escaped, so on Windows they carry doubled backslashes where interlock prints the path verbatim.
divergences.note: A consequence of D-0109 rather than a decision taken here, recorded because it is what makes two ported cases adapted.
